utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Case Number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Registrar, could we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Mathias Neuner and Daryl Mundis, assisted by our case manager, Mr. Andres Vatter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Could we have appearances for the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President, good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Mirna Milanovic, legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Amir Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, our legal assistant

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Trial Chamber would like to greet everyone present as well as the registrar who will be with us again today, as will the Prosecution, Defence counsel, the accused, and everyone else in the courtroom including the interpreters. We have to deal with the exhibits today, so I will give the floor to the Defence so that they can confirm that they want to tender into evidence the exhibits in the binders plus -- indicated in the binders, plus the map. Yes, you may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Defence counsel suggests that all the documents that were shown to the witness and that were recognised by the witness as his documents or documents from his own brigade and all documents in which he identified facts with regard to which he testified before this Trial Chamber and said that they were true facts, we suggest that all these documents be tendered into evidence. And in this list of documents, in Section 1, we suggest that 0439, 0515, 0526, 0531, 0730, 0773, 0776, 0970 be admitted into evidence. Under Section 2, we suggest that the following 0674 be admitted; 0797, 0831, 0832, 0842, 0873, 0971, 0976, 0981, 1001, 1011, 1013, 1014, 1020, 1037, 1053. We suggest that these be admitted into evidence. Under Section 3 are the documents we suggest be admitted into evidence: 0446, 0774, 0771, 0913. Under Section 4, we have evidence that was shown to the witness, but this was already admitted as Defence exhibits or as Prosecution exhibits. We also suggest that the map be admitted into evidence, which was used by the map in the course of the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. Does the Prosecution have any comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have no objection to the documents as listed by my learned colleague being admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar, could we have final exhibit numbers for these documents which will surely be the same ones, but we have the issue of the map to deal with.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. We will use the same numbers, in fact, so for the sake of the transcript, the first document, DH439; English version DH439/E. DH0515; the English version will be DH515/E. DH526; the English version will be DH526/E. DH531; the English version will be DH531/E. DH730 admitted into evidence, and the English version will DH730/E. DH773; English version DH773/E. DH776; the English version will be DH776/E. DH896; the English version will be DH896/E. Then we have the documents which were shown on the 22nd of October 2004, DH674 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, 970 is missing.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. I apologise, Mr. President. DH970; the English version will be DH970/E. And I will now continue. DH707; the English version will be DH707/E. DH797; the English version will be DH797/E. DH831; the English version 831/E. DH831/E. DH82; the English version will be 832/E. DH842; the English version will be DH842/E. DH873; it will be DH873/E for the English version. DH971; English version will be DH971/E. DH976; the English version will be DH976/E. DH986; the English version will be DH986/E. DH1001; the English version will be DH1001/E. DH1011; the English version will be DH1011/E. DH1013; the English version will be DH1013/E. DH1014; the English version will be DH1014/E. DH1020; the English version will be DH1020/E. DH1037; the English version will be DH1037/E. DH1053; the English version DH1053/E.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, in line 17, the first document, 614, you should mention it again because it isn't contained in the English transcript. Line 17, we have DH614 and a few dots and nothing else. So please, let's have another -- please mention the number again.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. DH674; the English version, in fact, will be DH674/E.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have four other documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] DH446; the English version will be DH446/E. DH704; the English version DH704/E. DH711; the English version DH711/E. DH913; the English version will be DH913/E. And there is the map that we still have to deal with. It was signed by the witness yesterday, and I suggest that we give it Exhibit Number DH341. This follows the numbers provided us by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Everyone has taken note of the exhibit numbers. There are no comments to be made. And I think the Prosecution has produced a document. Are they requesting that this document be admitted into evidence? Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The Prosecution would respectfully request that that document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Defence Counsel?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We stand by the comments we made in connection with this document, and we object to this document being admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Trial Chamber will render its decision after the break. And the other Defence team, any comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have no comments to make. We have no objections to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could very briefly. Perhaps it might be of benefit to the Trial Chamber as well as for the purposes of the transcript if one of my colleagues from the Hadzihasanovic team could briefly explain with respect to DH341 the overlay of the map, the markings that were made with respect to locating that on top of this map because there were certain marks that were made so that if in the future the parties or the Trial Chamber wishes that overlay to be placed back on the map, perhaps we can have both this map identified for the record as well as they can explain the hash marks that were made so that overlay corresponds to what the witness testified -- or the markings that the witness made. Otherwise, we might not be able to place the overlay in the precise locations corresponding to where the witness made the markings. I think that would be very helpful for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The witness added some indications, some markings on the map. Could the Defence counsel provide us with any clarifications so that it's recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As we know, at the request of the Defence, the witness drew the lines representing the Serbian forces. He used red to indicate them. And then the witness indicated the lines held by the BH Army. He drew these lines in blue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps the camera could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It doesn't matter. I thought it was the same map because we can't see very well from here.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness indicated HVO -- the positions of HVO forces in green. If you follow the transcript, it's possible to understand the map. Afterwards, the witness marked the command post of the 306th Brigade. He used an initial letter in our own language, and then he indicated the forward command post facing the Serbian forces. He also marked this position with the initial letter in our language, and he provided clarifications that are contained in the transcript. The witness then indicated the position of the headquarters of the commands of the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, and 4th Battalions. He also wrote 1B, which would mean the "1st Battalion." Then the witness encircled positions or places inhabited by Bosniaks and Croats. He encircled entities that were inhabited by Bosniaks. He marked these positions in blue, and positions inhabited by Croats were marked in green. And then he drew lines to indicate the territory under the full control of either the BH Army, and he indicated the territory under the full control of the HVO in green. And he also used green to indicate the permanent checkpoints, the permanent HVO checkpoints, and he marked these positions with the letter P to show that these checkpoints were permanent checkpoints manned by armed men. There were a number of such checkpoints, one on Ovnak as far as I can remember. I don't know where the others are. But this can be seen on the map and it can be understood on the basis of his testimony. And then he indicated temporary checkpoints which were set up in crisis situations. And he marked these positions with PP, which in our language would mean "temporary checkpoint." I think those were the main elements marked on the map, whereas everything else can be followed on the basis of the transcript. This is what the interpreter did yesterday when the witness marked the map on the basis of what he had said the other day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And also I think we should indicate that the overlay was used with respect to the 1 to 25.000 scale map that is mounted on a rather large piece of wood in the courtroom. And also, the witness made in the corners of the map some cross marks indicating I believe the grid reference points on the map so that the overlay can be positioned correctly on the map so that the lines are, in effect, in the correct position. He made several cross marks with the numerical indicators of the grid reference so that if the overlay is again placed on the map the numerical cross-references he made in the corners can be matched up with the grid references on the map so we have the overlay in the precise location on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this information. Mr. Registrar, we have been told that the number of the map will change. It won't be DH341 but DH342. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. President. The exhibit number of this map will in fact be DH342.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. DH342. Yes, you may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I just wanted to add something. In the course of our examination, the witness indicated the place called Maline. He used a full circle to mark this place, and he also marked the place called Hajderove Njive in a similar way. It was a circle which was coloured in. He indicated the road from Hajderove Njive to Maline, and he said that the distance was 12 kilometres between those two places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We take note of what you have said. We'll rule about -- on the Prosecution's request after the pause. We have two witnesses who have to be heard by the end of Thursday. One hour and a half has been scheduled for today's witness. Please don't go beyond the allocated time. I will now ask the usher to call the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. Are you receiving the interpretation of what I'm saying? If so, please say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the request of the Defence, you will be testifying today. Before you testify, you must take the solemn declaration. In order to do so, I would like you to tell me what your first and last names are, and could you also tell me your date of birth and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Hamed. My surname, Mesanovic. I was born on the 4th of August in 1950 in Travnik in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What position do you hold at the moment? Are you employed or are you retired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm employed. I work in the state organs of the administration of the Central Bosnian canton in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 and 1993, what position did you hold? That was over ten years ago.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina was committed, I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not asking you about that. I would like to know what your position was in 1992 and 1993. Were you a civilian? Were you a member of the military? What position did you hold? What duties did you perform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying to tell you about the period. I was the director of a state company in Travnik until the beginning of the aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina. Then I volunteered to join the Territorial Defence. And until the end of the war, in the course of 1992 and in the course of 1993, I was at the defence lines of the BH Army, or rather, prior to the formation of the BH Army, I was at the defence lines of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Did you have military rank or were you an ordinary soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the war started, I was 2nd lieutenant. I was conferred that rank in the former JNA. I left the JNA with that rank in 1974. I left the JNA with the rank of 2nd lieutenant. And towards the end of the war, I was conferred the rank of colonel. And that was the rank I had when the war ended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Have you already testified before an international or national court with regard to the events that occurred in 1992 and 1993, or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time that I will be testifying before an international court, and I have never testified before a national court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could you please read out the solemn declaration that the usher will show you. You can read it out now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to Defence counsel who will be examining you, I would like to provide you with some information, as I do whenever a witness comes to testify here. You have just taken a solemn declaration. You have sworn to speak the truth. That means that you can't give false testimony because in the case of false testimony you could be subject to a prosecution, to prosecution and sanctions possible in the case of false testimony. If a witness played a role in the field and provides information that could be used against the witness, you should be aware of the fact that when testifying, you're granted a form of immunity. So whatever you say cannot be used in any subsequent prosecution against you. Another important piece of information is that you will have to answer the questions that will be put to you. The Defence will conduct its examination-in-chief. And in the course of their examination, their questions will not be leading. Their questions must be neutral ones, and you should answer those questions. However, in the course of the cross-examination, the questions put to you can be formulated in a different manner. Try to answer to the best of your ability. If you fail to understand a question, because sometimes the questions can be very complicated, if you don't understand the question, ask the person putting the question to you to rephrase it. If any difficulties arise, inform the Trial Chamber of the fact. According to the Rules of this Tribunal, the Judges sitting before you may ask you at any point in time questions. The Judges may ask you questions to clarify some of your answers given to one of the parties, or if the Judges feel that some information is lacking, the Judges may want to ask you questions to obtain the missing information. But as a rule, if the appropriate questions are put to you by the parties, it won't be necessary for the Judges to put questions to you. The Judges will put questions to you only if this is in the interests of justice. So roughly speaking, this is how your testimony will proceed. And if everything goes as planned, it should be over today. You won't have to stay here for a number of days. Without wasting any more time, we have about one hour left before the break. I will now give the floor to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mesanovic.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Defence Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have told us where and when you were born. Can you please tell us where you lived after that.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I lived in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, you must have noticed that everything you say is being interpreted, and that's why you paused. I'm going to ask you to make a break, a little pause between my question and your answer. This will help the interpreters interpret you, and everybody in the courtroom will be able to follow your answers. Did you understand that?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You have also told us that you left the JNA when the rank of the 2nd lieutenant. Before the war, did you have a war assignment; and if so, where was that?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: When I left the JNA where I completed the school for reserve officers of the infantry.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You may continue.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I received the rank of the 2nd lieutenant, and I was assigned to the reserve units of the JNA. When I obtained my assignment, I was supposed to go for training and for lectures, but I didn't like the army and I avoided the training and the lectures. And that's why I did not get promotion in the reserve.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Since you lived in Travnik, can you tell us who was it who lived in Travnik and what was the relationship like between the inhabitants of Travnik before the war.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Before the war, according to the 1991 census, there were about 50 per cent Bosniaks, about 41 to 43 per cent Croats, and 7 per cent Serbs. There were also some other minorities in Travnik. And the urban area of Travnik had about 18.000 inhabitants, and the entire municipality had about 70.000 inhabitants. All this is according to the 1991 census. We all lived in harmony, as brothers. We visited each other. We were godmothers and godfathers to our children, and we celebrated our religious holidays with each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I believe this will suffice for us to understand the situation. Mr. Mesanovic, can you tell us in the years -- in the 1990s, did any changes occur and what kind of changes were those?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: In the 1990s, the former Yugoslavia started breaking up. New parties were formed. The fight for power started among the parties. And the system of power and the functioning of the state administration started to change.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After these changes, who was given the power in Travnik? Who won the power in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Two parties, the SDA and the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, in 1991, were there some developments taking place in the former Yugoslavia which had an impact on the situation in Travnik? If that was the case, can you please briefly explain what this was all about.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I have already said that there was a gradual dissolution of the former Yugoslavia, and this is all well known. And war started in certain parts of the former Yugoslavia. The JNA units started withdrawing from everywhere else, and some of those units arrived in the town of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have already responded to the question put to you by the President of the Chamber, and you said that at the beginning of 1992, you volunteered to join the Territorial Defence. Please tell us: When exactly did you join the Territorial Defence, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: It was in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Why did you join the TO?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The developments in Yugoslavia, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and in the general area of Travnik indicated to me that the situation is becoming more unfavourable for this area. In the Vlasic plateau, units of the JNA became stationed. They took certain positions, and their excuse was that they were carrying out military manoeuvres. They banned passage and arrival at Vlasic. I had a weekend cottage in Babanovac, and I couldn't reach it because I had to go through Mount Vlasic. When I wanted to pass through, I was stopped at a checkpoint. That's the first time I saw people wearing Chetnik uniforms. Members of the Croatian people established their own military formations or groups.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So these are the reasons that prompted you?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. People came from Croatia with arms. They started moving around town. And the only way for me to do my bit to the survival of Bosnia-Herzegovina is to join the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, at that moment, was there an armed force that was a legitimate and legal force of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, when Bosnia-Herzegovina was proclaimed as an independent state, the only legal force of Bosnia-Herzegovina was the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have told us that you joined voluntarily. At that moment, did you have a certain duty or position in the Territorial Defence; and if that is the case, what position was that?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Since I was a reserve officer of the former JNA, and since I have a degree in law and I had spent a lot of time working in the state administration, I enjoyed certain reputation and respect in town. And they asked me to become the commander of the regional staff. This was proposed to me by Zijad Sehic, the then commander of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the regional staff is. What units would be under its control or in its strength?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The municipal staff consisted of regional staffs and detachments which were deployed in certain parts of the municipality in accordance with the mobilisation plan. I was supposed to take over the regional staff of Travnik; that is, the town, the urban region, and I was supposed to link up some units which were there in particular neighbourhoods. Those were groups of people who rallied together to defend their homes. Those were spontaneous rallies. And I was supposed to cover that particular area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, how long did you remain in the position of the commander of the regional staff; and what positions did you held [as interpreted] in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina up to the end of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't know whether there is any other word to translate this, but I believe that there is a mistake in the interpretation. The regional staff has been translated as regional staff. It is possible that this is the right interpretation; however, so far we have been talking about district staff. So I would kindly ask the interpreters to make a distinction to that effect. This is just my objection to the transcript. So the regional -- the district staff is smaller than the municipal staff, and the regional staff is a bigger -- covers a bigger area than the municipal area. Can we please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the position of the district staff, and what are the positions that you held up to the end of 1993? Can you please give us your answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I remained in the position of the commander of the district staff up to November 1993. At that moment, brigades were established.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What year was that?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: It was 1993. I'm sorry, I'm sorry, I apologise. 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. We are still having mistakes in the transcript. Can we have your answer again. I don't want to interpret your answers. You said that you became the commander of the regional staff. What is the regional staff and what its superior command?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I became the commander of the district staff in April 1992. The district staff covers the area of the urban part of Travnik. Its superior command is the municipal staff of the Territorial Defence, with its headquarters in Travnik as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a problem in the interpretation. When the witness says "staff," in French, the translation is "sectoriel," and in the English the translation is "district" when he mentioned the regional staff. So he is not the chief of the regional staff; his position was localised, and it covered the town of Travnik. Isn't that the case? You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you can see, there are some additional problems. I may be leading you, but can you tell us whether your district staff was only one of the units of the municipal staff?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Which was your superior command? Who was it?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The municipal staff of the Territorial Defence of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And which was the superior command to the municipal staff?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The regional staff of the Territorial Defence headquartered in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you became the commander of the district staff in Travnik, in the town of Travnik, in April and remained in that position up to November 1992. What duties and positions did you occupy in the BiH Army after that?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I became the chief of the municipal staff of TO Travnik. I remained in that position until the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before you became the chief of the municipal staff, did you have more complete information about what the Territorial Defence was within the overall system of defence?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was fully informed. When Bosnia and Herzegovina was recognised as an independent state, the Territorial Defence was proclaimed the official armed force, military force, excluding the police, the official armed force of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and its task was to defend Bosnia and Herzegovina from any form of aggression.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the moment when you joined the Territorial Defence, you, as the commander initially of the district staff and then of the municipal staff, were you aware of the equipment that the municipal staff and the municipal Territorial Defence had at their disposal?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I know it very well. When Zijad Caber appointed me the commander of the district staff of the Travnik TO, he did not place anything at my disposal. I didn't have manpower. I didn't have arms. I didn't have any equipment. Then I called a couple of my friends. I persuaded them to join the defence. And together with them, I established my command. We based our command in the premises of a company, and then we started visiting those spontaneously gathered and rallied people to try to persuade them to join us because we were the only official military formation. We told them that should they not join us, that they would be considered paramilitaries. And then we used the public media, that is, the Radio Travnik, to broadcast our information on taking conscripts for the TO.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How many weapons did you have?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: We started with six barrels, six hunting rifles that were my own. And then we went to Travnik and purchased from a Croat. I know that his name is Marinko. He was the owner of a coffee bar. We bought two Zagis from him. It was the first time I ever saw that type of weapon. I am following the transcript. And then I made a list of all the weapons that the population had, that they had purchased on the black market. So at the beginning, we had a total of some 20 barrels.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said, Mr. Mesanovic, that you approached those groups and asked them to join the TO. In the former system, who was responsible for mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: In the former system, the body responsible for mobilisation was the secretary for national defence, and it was a municipal administration body.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How come that mobilisation was not carried out in keeping with the mobilisation plans that existed at the time?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: It was impossible for several reasons. Firstly, when the power and positions within parties were divided among the parties -- the parties being the HDZ and the SDA -- the secretary of national defence became a Croat. Everything that was on the strength of the reserve force of the JNA and of the TO was mixed population which reflected the breakdown of the Travnik population before the war. So it consisted of Bosniaks, Serbs, and Croats. Some of the Serbs moved to the territory which was already under the control of the former JNA, and some of the Croats joined the HVO. At that time, they were not called the HVO. They were called the Croatian Army. And there were some other units organised by Croats such as the HOS. So it was impossible to carry out mobilisation in keeping with the prescribed procedure and regulations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have briefly explained the situation that you faced as the commander of the district staff. And now, can you please tell us, at the time when you were facing such circumstances, were there some combat activities taking place in Travnik? And if that was the case, what was the combat situation like?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The Serbian and Montenegrin aggressors started being active on the territory of Travnik in several ways. First they started expelling Bosniak and Croatian population from the parts of the territories that they had occupied. Then open combat action started against Travnik, more specifically Turbe and the Biljani region. At that time, they took the highest peak of Mount Vlasic, Biljanski, which had been guarded by the police force.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The onslaught of the Serbian forces, where was it stopped with respect to the town of Travnik?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: This was stopped in the region of Turbe, in the region of Karaula village, Sesici village, in the region of the Sesic mount [as interpreted] where the regional staff of Travnik had its position, so that means my men were there. And then the villages of Potkraj, Secevo, Paklarevo. Towards Travnik and towards the Bila Valley, towards Neokrnje, not easy to describe. But in brief outlines, this is where the defence lines were put up.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, can you tell us briefly with regard to such a military situation and the situation with the legal defence forces, what was the situation in the town itself and whether this situation in a certain way had an impact on the establishment of defence units.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The situation in town was very chaotic. A lot of refugees came from Bosanska Krajina. Those were people who had been expelled by the Serbs and Montenegrins. They arrived in buses, cargo trucks. They would be transported to our positions. Then we would stop our combat activities. The separation line was about 3 to 4 kilometres wide. And these people were sent to us on foot, to the town of Travnik. Very often, they would strip them naked, and they would be sent to us naked in huge numbers. Very often, it would occur that they would separate girls and women from the rest of the groups, and they would take them in an unknown direction. They would separate them from their families, and they would send the families off to Travnik. Those people were taken care of in the town of Travnik. And at times, there were between 10 and 15.000 of them. And I told at the very beginning that the town itself had no more than 16.000 inhabitants. There were a lot of armed groups moving about the town of Travnik. There were our members, members of the Territorial Defence. There were members of the Croatian Defence Council. There were the Croatian armed forces, which did not cooperate with anybody. They were separate military groups. There was the civilian police. And the refugees from certain towns and regions that had arrived in Travnik started establishing their own bodies of power. I'm not talking about the territorial administration, but organisational administration, and they formed their own police stations, for example. We had the CSB Banja Luka, the Security Services Centre of Banja Luka. The organised units arrived from Krajina, the 1st and the 7th Brigade which were stationed in the town of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, in 1992 and 1993, who had power in Travnik? What were the legal authorities in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: For me, the legal organs of power, at the time and now, were the legally elected organs of power. That's as far as the civilian structures are concerned. We had the municipal assembly of Travnik, and there was the police under their control as well as the civilian protection. The legal organs of power in the military sense consisted of the Territorial Defence. But at the same time, that these legal organs of power were formed, the power organs of Herceg Bosna were formed. A decree was issued. They established their own organs of power. They threatened the legal organs of power. They said they could participate in power, but, let's say, under the organs of Herceg Bosna. We were told that we Bosniaks could join the organs of power of Herceg Bosna. The authorities in Sarajevo immediately issued a decree declaring all organs of power of Herceg Bosna to be invalid. We attempted to solve that problem. I personally didn't participate in those attempts as far as the civilian structures were concerned. But I know there were meetings, and we tried to establish common institutions, common organs of power. We tried to form a joint army. We tried to defend Travnik because the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressor was threatening our defence lines. And if Travnik fell, the entire Lasva valley would be threatened as well as Vitez, Novi Travnik, and Zenica. These towns would be surrounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, thank you. Let me now ask you the following: Given the function of the legal civilian authorities and the functions of the war presidency, could you tell me whether the Territorial Defence in 1992 and later, whether the BH Army had any control over the civilian organs of power?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No, it didn't have any control over them. And according to the regulations, it wasn't possible for them to have such control.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you have already said that in 1993 you were the chief of the municipal staff, could you tell me whether the commander of the staff was a member of the Travnik Municipality War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I could elaborate on this as I spent my entire career -- almost my entire career in the state organs, working in state organs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But don't go into too many details.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Before the war, and before the new authorities were established on the basis of the elections, the war presidency was composed of the president of the municipal assembly; his deputy; the president of the executive committee of the municipality; the presidents of local councils; presidents of social organisations, the social and political organs; the commander of the barracks; the commander of the municipal staff of the Territorial Defence; the commander of the civilian protection; and the secretary of the secretariat for national defence. After the elections this system no longer functioned, for the simple reason that we didn't have social or political associations. We didn't have municipal councils. So the war presidency was composed by the chief of the municipality, the presidents of clubs, the secretary of the secretariat for national defence, and the secretary for the Ministry of the Interior. The commander of the municipal staff of the Territorial Defence wasn't in the war presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, since the Territorial Defence is an armed force, it became separate from certain organs of civilian power in this manner. Could you tell me whether you have information about how the civilian authorities accepted the fact that they did not have absolute control over the Territorial Defence. Do you have any information about this?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was very difficult for them to accept this. They wanted to have a constant overview of the military situation; they wanted to be in command of military structures in a certain sense. Very frequently, they would go to the defence lines and take cigarettes to the soldiers. This is as far as my units are concerned. When distributing cigarettes -- because cigarettes were the greatest problem in the war -- when distributing cigarettes, they would say, If your commander can't provide you with cigarettes, well, we have brought cigarettes for you so that you can know who is taking care of you, so that you can know who is thinking about you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: We won't go into that now. But did the civilian organs have any responsibilities with regard to the army? And if that was the case, what were they obliged to do in order to make sure that the army could function as necessary?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: They had to provide logistical support for the army. That was their duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like you to be shown a series of documents now. The series of document that you have before you, have a look at the section entitled "Other Documents." It's in the second half of the bundle. There's a divider, and you'll see at the top the title "Other Documents."

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: "Other documents."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have a look at document number 4, and then number 6, and then I will have some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just clarify something. Number 4, that's the decision you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It has the number 0853 at the top. And there's number 6, and the number at the top of the document is 0912.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If you've had a look at the first document, the decision, it's a decision taken by the war presidency on the 8th of April, tell me whether this decision reflects what you were talking about a minute ago. The civilian organs of power wanted to get involved in the army's duties?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I haven't seen this decision before. But this is a typical example of the attempts to meddle with army responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at Document Number 6 now. It's a decision from the war presidency.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Husein Delic is, the person mentioned in the decision?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know this gentleman. He works in the Ministry of the Interior in Travnik today, these days, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Does the document you have before you indicate the responsibilities that the civilian authorities had with regard to the regular police force?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is in accordance with the regulations. And the responsibility of the war presidency at that time, that is to say, of the civilian authorities, was to appoint members of the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me: Since in response to a prior question you said that sometime in November you took over a new position, could you tell me whether at some time in 1992, there were certain organisational changes made to the army structure, army organisation. And if so, could you tell me what sort of changes were made, and could you again tell me of the position that you assumed.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: At a briefing that was held in the municipal staff, and I as a commander of the district staff attended it, we were told that the Territorial Defence would be reorganised, and that brigades should be established. Units of the Travnik district staff were to become part of the newly established 312th Brigade in Travnik. As brigade commander, Zijad Caber was appointed, and I was to take over the position of chief of the Territorial Defence municipal staff.\

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the municipal staff at the time?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, the commander of the municipal staff was Mr. Ribo Haso.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And what was the role of the municipal staff, then? If you could explain this to us briefly. What sort of forces did it have at its disposal?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just provide a clarification: Why do I emphasise -- why do I point out to Mr. Caber and Mr. Ribo? Why do I emphasise the title Mr.? At the time, there were no ranks, so everyone was called Mr. On the basis of the instructions we received and on the basis of the documents we had, the municipal staff was supposed to form two anti-sabotage detachments to protect features of military importance from being sabotaged.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you form these units? What sort of equipment did you have?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: When I was the chief of the municipal staff, Ahmed Kulenovic was appointed as commander. He was a professional officer from the former JNA. And we tried to carry out the order, but we were never able to do so because brigades were given priority when it came to recruitment. And they were never up to strength in accordance with the establishment. So we weren't able to form anti-sabotage detachments. As far as weapons are concerned, all the weapons were handed over to the brigade. We just took over my hunting weapon to the municipal staff, and I know that two combatants came from Vitez. They brought automatic rifles, and they joined the municipal staff. Those are weapons that we had, and we used these weapons to protect the command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My colleagues have just pointed out - because I'm not listening to the French interpretation - they have pointed out that the French interpretation of what you have called anti-sabotage detachment is a sabotage detachment. They have translated it as sabotage detachment, whereas the interpretation into English is correct. So could the interpreters please take this into account. Thank you. Mr. Mesanovic, I apologise for having interrupted you. You were mentioning the weapons you had. What sort of men was the municipal staff composed of at the time? Who was in the municipal staff?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, I don't know the exact number. But we had about 100 men, more or less. These were handicapped men, disabled men, or men who weren't able-bodied men so they couldn't join brigades. We used them as guards. So they did not join these anti-sabotage detachments.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please have a look at another document in the same bundle, in Section 2 under number 5.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: 1102. Is that the one you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: 0880 is the document I'm referring to. It's under "Other Documents" and it's after number 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have a look at it, please.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: You're thinking about item 4?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This document is dated the 17th of April. Does it reflect what you have just mentioned? "The men of which the municipal staff was composed."

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document signed by General Mehmed Alagic, and on the basis of a report or rather on the basis of information about the actual situation in the field.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me whether the municipal staff at the time had a military police unit as one of its organs?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No. It didn't have a military police force, nor was it in a position to have such a force given its establishment and the regulations. And that was the reality. We did not have a military police force.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, could you please have a look at Document Number 1. 0530, and that's in Section 2. And in Section 3, have a look at Document 0708.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've had a look at these documents. Do you have a question you'd like to ask me?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Document 0530 and Document 0708, do these documents reflect what you've just testified about? That is to say, whether there was a military police force within the municipal staff?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this document is dated the 19th of December 1992. And this document explains that the military police which used to be part of the municipal staff was becoming part of the 312th Mountain Brigade, and that is what is done. I don't know whether some of these men went to join other units, but I know that the commander and most of the men joined the 312th Brigade. And here we can see that in Document 0708 that the military police was assigned to certain units, and this is, in fact, what was done.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, could we now move on to some questions that have to do with another field. You said that the HVO was formed and certain other armed forces. Could you tell me whether there were any problems and if so what sort of problems were caused in Travnik by the fact that a parallel military structure had been established. And you, as part of the Territorial Defence or you in the municipal staff, did you take any measures to deal with the situation? If you know anything about this, could you please tell us what you know.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The existence of a parallel military structure caused very serious problems as far as the BH Army is concerned. Above all, the HVO had well-armed troops. They were all in uniform. They had good logistical supplies, and they had very experienced combatants from the battlefield in Croatia. As they immediately said that we represented a military force that they did not recognise, this caused us serious problems. I personally had problems at the line from Turbe when we were -- where we were holding positions for a certain period of time. They kept driving my troops away from the lines. They would insult them. They would say that they were a paramilitary formation. In the town itself, there were verbal conflicts and conflicts of other kinds between various groups and our members. And after a certain period of time, they started setting up checkpoints. Rather, they immediately set up checkpoints in the territory where they had inhabited places. I'm referring to the municipality. And initially, they would let our units pass through, but this depended on their goodwill. Later, they made it necessary to have permits, so we would have to inform them in advance. We would have to tell them about our forces, about the vehicles we had, about the weapons we had. And if something was not correct with regard to the permits, they would send men back. And in parts of the municipality, not the part under my control, they would also stop civilian buses, and they would drive away the soldiers from the buses who were going to lines. They would disarm them. There were also physical assaults so that I as the commander of the district staff and then as the chief of the municipal staff had to have frequent contact with their command in order to deal with certain problems and in order to avoid clashes. These discussions were very difficult, although I know that we were not guilty, were not responsible, we had to apologise. And I was even disarmed at a checkpoint together with my deputy, the late Hasan Sefer who was killed in combat later on. They lined us up against a wall and pointed their guns at us. They disarmed us. They threatened and insulted us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please have a look at the document in Section 1 under number 1. And the Defence number is 0513. It is dated the 3rd of December 1992. Could you please tell me, since the second paragraph states that the military and political situation in the territory of Herceg Bosna is ever-more complex and in particular in Vitez, Novi Travnik, Travnik and Gornji Vakuf, tell me whether this reflects the situation that you had in Travnik. If you have a look at the items in this document from the 3rd Corps, does the document reflect the situation?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise the situation. But this is a very brief description of the situation which was, in fact, far more serious.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please have a look under the section entitled "Other Documents." Have a look at Document 2. Defence number 0656. And after having a look at the document, could you tell me whether this is one of the ways in which you attempted to avoid conflict with the HVO, and in particular, an armed conflict with the HVO. The document is entitled "Information for the Public." And I would first like to ask you whether you know who signed this document.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: This document was signed by Ahmed Kulenovic, the Army of -- the commander of the municipal staff. And it was also signed by Colonel Filip Filipovic, the commander of the Travnik Brigade. The fact that the document was signed by them, well, Ahmed Kulenovic signed it as Zapovjednik, which is a Croatian word for commander. It is not the word that we used. These measures had been agreed on, and the HVO and Colonel Filip Filipovic, who was a good friend of mine during and after the war, signed this pro forma. We adhered to these regulations. And as a result, we had quite a few problems with the army because it's very difficult to explain to a soldier that the soldier should not take revenge, that he should not use force to respond to force. If his sister or wife were maltreated and imprisoned, it was difficult to explain this to them. And very often, our soldiers would say that we were traitors, that we had betrayed the Bosniak people and that we had taken sides with the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, perhaps this would be a good time to have a break. I could continue after the break, if you agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's necessary to have our technical break now. I'd like to point out to the Defence that they have about half an hour left for their examination-in-chief. We will resume at 5 to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to the Defence, the Chamber has decided on the admissibility of the document that was tendered by the Prosecution. And the Chamber has decided to have the document admitted. Can we have a number, Mr. Registrar, for this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The number is P931.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Ms. Residovic, you may proceed. You have a half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, you were talking about the relationship with the HVO. I'm going to show you a number of documents. Please tell me whether you are familiar with these documents or whether you're familiar with the facts contained in these documents. And after that, I'm going to ask you questions only in reference to two documents. Under 1, where it says "Relation with the HVO." Can you please look after tab 2. This is Document 0823, Defence Document 0823.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the document?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The document under number 4, 0843, are you familiar with the document?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the document, but I am -- I am aware of the contents.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Document under 15, are you familiar with the event described in this document?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I see the document for the first time, but I'm familiar with the event.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Document under 18, 0902.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: These are regular reports that were sent regularly. I may have seen it. This is just a description of certain events.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the last part of the binder under the title "Exhibits", can you please look at the document under number 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, 0603. Does this document reflect the situation with the equipment in the district staff, in the municipal staff?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is what was emphasised in all of our communication.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at Document 4, Document 5, Document 6. Again, are you familiar with the events described in these documents?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Document 1083, I am familiar with it. I was involved in dealing with the problem of this skyscraper or high-rise building.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: 1102, are you familiar with this event?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with the event. And this fire was opened on the command of the Territorial Defence staff in Travnik. I was just being visited by UNPROFOR units. Fire was opened on them, so they had to seek shelter in the courtyard of my command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, document under 6, 1128. Does this document speak of facts that you are personally familiar with?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have the time to read it, but at first glance, yes. It is about the resettlement of the Croatian population which was done under the pressure of the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can we go back to number 4. You said that you were personally involved in dealing with the problem. The document is 1083. Can you describe the event for us. And how were you involved?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm looking at the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm waiting for my turn to speak. Members of the HVO stated that from a high-rise building in Kalibunar inhabited by civilians, fire was being opened constantly on their positions, and that on the top of the high-rise building there is an anti-aircraft gun which also opened fire. In my telephone contact with the inhabitants of that building, they asked for my help. They said that they came under attack, that they put their women and children in the basement, that the pressure is too high to bear, that an ultimatum was given to him to surrender. I got in contact with the contact and some officers of the HVO. We came to the spot. We inspected all the flats and the roof, and we were able to state that there were no arms and that this was nothing but an attack on a civilian building. And the situation was calm for a while. However, one thing led to another. There were more problems that arose from that, and it turned into a fully blown conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Document under 6, which had to do with the resettlement of the Croatian population. The number is 1108. What do you personally know about this document? What do you know about these events? The number is 1128.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The HVO units first moved their command structures from the town. They left some buildings. Although in the basement of the PTT building, we had our joint command before that. Then they took positions in Jankovici village. Actually, they didn't take positions. They put their command there. All this time, there were incidents across the area. We tried to deal with those incidents together through negotiations. And eventually, we were informed that there was a massive exodus of the Croatian population towards the Vlasic plateau. We asked them what this was all about. They said they didn't know. They said they would go and inspect and they never came back. Later on, when we inspected the area, it was not me personally who did that, but I received information from the others who did. We received information that people in cars and on foot escorted by armed soldiers started moving towards Mount Vlasic, towards the Serbian positions. And later on, we received information that a Serbian armoured vehicle entered the sector of this area that was abandoned by the Croatians. We thought that the Serbian forces had taken over the HVO lines. Commander Alagic spoke to that effect on Radio Travnik and said that the Croatian fighters had ceded their positions in favour of the Serbian forces. However, by our reconnaissance we established that the Serbian forces had not taken the positions so we infiltrated our units and put up our defence line. This is the line that the HVO had manned facing the Serbs and the Montenegrins. And if we hadn't taken those lines, this would lead to the fall of the town of Travnik. Later on in some contacts with our friends, Croats, they told that they were forced to leave their homes. Some families had remained, but very few. But these people told us that they were forced in an organised manner at gunpoint to leave towards the Serbian territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the briefly at the following three documents. One is under 13. It's number is 0824. Documents under 16, and document under 17. These are HVO documents.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've had a look.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you testified about the efforts that you made as the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Territorial Defence staff in order to avoid conflicts, and you also testified that the HVO participated in talks and did differently, do these documents testify to the behaviour of the HVO which was contrary to any efforts in dealing with the situation? Is this your personal knowledge, and is it your testimony that the HVO behaved in the way described in these documents? Can you please not be guided by the contents of these documents, but rather share with us your personal knowledge from the year 1992. Do these documents show that the HVO --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. It's both leading and compound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Try to rephrase your question, Ms. Residovic, so as to make it not leading. I know that you are battling against the time, and you're trying to gain time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, tell me what you knew about the behaviour of the HVO in Travnik. Is that reflected in the three documents that I have just shown you?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I have never seen these documents before. I don't have the time to read them carefully. But I am now very moved when I look at these documents. I didn't know that this was regulated in this way. And this is a true reflection of the behaviour of the HVO. I used to call them extremist groups. I used to tell them that their extremists did not obey orders, that they didn't respect our agreements, that their extremists had to be stopped, that there would be a conflict, that there would be a blood battle, a bloodbath, that the Serbs and Montenegrins would take our town, that we would all die. However, I can see now that this was part of their politics. I apologise, I don't know what else to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please allow me -- can you continue?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let's move on to some other issues with have nothing to do with the HVO. At one moment in Travnik, did some foreigners appear who were not locals of the former Yugoslavia? And did you see them? Who were they?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I feel the need to say that Mr. Drago Bilandzija participated in negotiations with me. I respected him. He was a member of the government, and this is the kind of decision that he made. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: We understand, and we appreciate. However, let's move on to other issues. I asked you whether in 1992 and 1993 in Travnik you noticed some people who were not locals of the former Yugoslavia. Who were they?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the BritBat that came to Travnik, and they approached me upon their arrival, there were many humanitarian organisations that had contacts with the civilian structures. There were a lot of foreigners. There were a lot of journalists. All the journalists who came to the municipality reported to us and to the HVO. They sought ways to go to the defence lines, to conduct interviews, and to be able to do their stories for which they were there. There were a lot of foreigners who moved about in Travnik who were -- who came from abroad.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you notice the arrival of some people from African and Asian countries, primarily from Arabic states?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I noticed mostly because of the way they dressed. They were dressed in traditional Arabic clothes. And as for the different colour of skin, it was not a surprise to me. I used to travel a lot before the war, so a different skin colour did not surprise me. I was somewhat startled by their attire. They were members of the humanitarian organisations. They usually moved in the lower part of the town, in the municipality. I was bound to see them because they moved between my command and the building where I resided.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see these persons carrying arms and did these persons come to your district staff?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: They didn't come to the district staff, never. I never saw them carrying arms, either.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally, or maybe at some meetings in the municipal staff learn that there were some individuals from African and Asian countries who -- did you ever hear that there were such persons who would be members of some of the Territorial Defence units or municipal staff units?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: In the municipal staff and in the Territorial Defence, there were no such persons like the ones you have mentioned in your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In 1993, did you have any personal information about some units of the Territorial Defence or municipal staff logistically supporting such groups of foreigners or individuals from foreign countries who had arrived in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Your question sounds very strange to me. We relied on civilian structures for logistical support. So there was no way for us to be -- provide logistical support to somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, at any moment in 1992 or 1993, were the Muslim forces established in Travnik? And if you know anything about that, can you share that information with us.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I know that the Bosniak Muslims established a unit which was located in the lower part of the town, in the furniture store called Medresa.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was this a unit established by the municipal staff? Who was it who established this unit?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The municipal staff did not establish it. It couldn't establish it. Such a unit would not have been part of our overall establishment. I don't know who was it who established it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, let me ask you a few more questions pertaining to a different area -- region. You were a member of the BiH Army, and as such you were bound to respect the international humanitarian law. Can you please tell us: How did you in the district staff, in the municipal staff where you were chief in 1993, and according to your information in the BiH Army, how did you inform your men about the obligations arising from that particular area?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I hold a degree in law, and I'm very well informed about the international law. From day one when I joined the army, that is, the Territorial Defence, I was the one who gathered volunteers. I have to emphasise that members of my units were Croats, Serbs, and Bosniaks. It was a mixed unit in that sense. Most of the unit members who joined me at the beginning of the war stayed with me until the end of the war. It's -- of course, those who survived. All the men that joined us with whom I spoke and whom I sent to the lines, I warned about the obligation to respect the Geneva Conventions. I told them how to treat civilians, how to treat prisoners, how to treat property. And this is what I did not only as the commander of the district staff but in all the positions that I held later on. And this is all documented by my written orders. Every written order that I issued in respect of combat activities contained the way my men should behave towards civilians and towards their property. And I would like to emphasise that in my zone of responsibility, in my staff we did not have any cases of looting and ill treatment of civilians. I have arguments. I have proof. I have people who will testify to the fact that we behaved or obeyed the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the document under number 12 and tell us whether you are familiar with this event.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm familiar with these developments. As far as the criminal charges are concerned, I don't know about this particular one. But we had a lot of criminal reports that were filed, either spontaneously or through the orders that we received from our superior command. We filed criminal reports in respect of all the members of the BH Army who perpetrated crimes. This on-site inspection by the public security station, I mentioned here towards the end. I'm familiar with this particular case, and I know that an on-site inspection was carried out, although I myself have never seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was the treatment of religious buildings? How did your units treat religious buildings, and what was the relationship that or attitude that the BH Army had towards religious buildings and their protection during the war?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The protection of religious and cultural buildings was the authority of civilian structures, and they did put in place some measures of protection, of physical protection. They provided security for some of the buildings. The position of the BiH Army - and I am talking from the point of view of our region, the Municipality of Travnik - we were very strict in those terms. There was no destruction of any religious building. I can share some of my experiences with you. For example, when we were in combat with the HVO facing this Vitez, the church in Donja Puticevo was some 10 or 15 metres behind the front line of the BiH Army. I was -- I went to the convent in Travnik. I asked to see the priest. I asked him to inspect the church together with me. There was an organ in the church. There were a lot of religious objects. Nothing had been touched, nothing had been plundered, save for one window that was broken by a bullet. It had been shot at from the HVO side. The priest came with me. He had trusted me, and he had known me from our previous contacts. We visited the church. He said that the church was valuable, but that they didn't have the means to protect it. I gave him a car to move all the valuable objects to the convent. While the army was there, I told him the whole thing was safe. However, when the army moved on, civilians would come, and it would be very difficult to protect anything. During combat activities in Gornji Dolac, I was informed that the priest and a few nuns, I don't know how many in the church, maybe a dozen of them had packed their things. They were standing in the church. They asked me what to do with them. I told them that nothing should happen to these people, that these people should be protected, that these people should not be insulted or ill treated and eventually they should be brought to Travnik. I spoke to them personally and they told me they wanted to go to Vitez. I told them there was combat going on towards Vitez, and I told them I couldn't help them. I asked them whether they would go to Travnik, and they said that they would go to the convent if that still existed. I asked for -- to be put through to the convent. I gave them the number. I told them to call himself, and that's where they went and they stayed there until the end of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was the attitude towards wounded enemy soldiers, for example? Wounded HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when HVO soldiers were wounded or imprisoned, they were treated in accordance with the Geneva Conventions. We would take wounded soldiers to the hospital in Travnik to be provided with medical treatment. I can give you an example. On the second day of the conflict, my daughter was wounded. She was in the fourth class of primary school at the time, so she was about 10 or 11 years old. She was seriously wounded in the leg, stomach, and in the back. She was bleeding. I was told to go to the hospital immediately. They didn't say that she was wounded. They said I should come, that they needed me for some reason. I went there, and you know, it's not nice when you see your child in such a condition. I asked the doctor whether she would survive. He said "If I had been wounded in this way, I wouldn't have had any chances," but she did. And then a wounded Croatian soldier that had been hit in the kidney was brought in. The doctor said he had priority because there was only one surgical ward. I said "You should decide about this. If he's a soldier and he has priority then my daughter will wait." If my daughter had died, I don't know how I would have felt today. But luckily, she survived and she is now studying in Vienna.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. As my time has expired, will you allow me to ask the witness one more question?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, after the questions I have put to you and your answers were very detailed, and sometimes your answers were quite emotional when you were talking about what you experienced in 1992 and 1993, my question is: What sort of difficulties were there in creating an army and establishing a system of command and control? What sort of difficulties did you encounter in 1992 and 1993 as an officer in the BH Army with regard to creating the army and establishing command and control?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: We encountered great difficulties. I was aware of the fact that I was defending my family and my own life, and only then that I was also defending the town and Bosnia and Herzegovina. I wasn't in a position to mount a defence on my own. I had to include as many people as possible in this defence. This was my position. I persuaded people to take up arms, to go to the lines. War is a terrible thing. I'd take a hundred and fifty armed men who were leaving their homes for the first time. They would go into a forest. The situation was unfamiliar. It was cold. And they might be shelled, they might die, they might be wounded. If one person is wounded, if one person is killed, this spread such fear among the men at the lines that all the men will leave the trenches. I'm talking about the initial stages, until these combatants became inured to death, to being wounded. We would carry out preparations throughout the night with certain units in order to persuade them to go to the line.
