They would complain that they didn't have food or their families had nothing to eat. They would say that they didn't have any cigarettes. They would say that they weren't adequately armed. We held one line -- I'll provide you with an example. When there was an attack from Vitez, an order was issued from Commander Alagic according to which we should leave all combatants with five bullets. And that the -- anything extra was to be used to provide additional support at the defence lines. I said that some families might file a report against me after the war because I sent their sons, their children to the lines without sufficient ammunition. They would say that I was the reason for which they had been wounded or for which they had been killed. Furthermore, we had problems with the HVO which would stop people. They wouldn't allow rotation to take place because not all the people lived in the town. They lived in the surrounding villages. From the Vlasic plateau, I had a unit. These were people who had been expelled and I used them to form a unit. Some of them lived in Vitez --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mesanovic. I just wanted you to tell us a little about those problems. And finally, as an officer who became an officer in the BH Army as a result of the conditions that prevailed, do you believe that you did everything you could to form an army, to mount a defence, and to take measures to ensure that no negative acts [Realtime transcript read in error: "negative acts"] were committed in your area?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I have said that I carried out the duties I had assigned myself in an honourable and honest manner. I didn't see the war as an opportunity to get rich. I didn't see the war as an opportunity to get involved in business of some kind or to get involved in illegitimate actions. For me, the purpose of war was to defend myself, as I said, and I should also point out that I attempted to make sure that all those in my vicinity acted in an honourable way, and I shall attempt to do this in the future, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. This concludes my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will now give the floor to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe Mr. Kubura's Defence would go first. But there is a problem with the transcript that I would like to try to correct before it disappears. I believe the final question that my learned colleague asked, the last phrase was "to ensure that no negative acts were committed in your area," rather than "negative acts were committed in your area." I may be mistaken, but I believe the word "no" should be before "negative acts" in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think my colleague is right. Perhaps it's an interpretation error. I said "to take measures to ensure that no negative acts or rather crimes were committed."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Does the Defence team for General Kubura have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we don't have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Does Mr. Mundis have any cross-examination to conduct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We have a few questions, Mr. President. I believe we'll be finished, hopefully, before the next break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness -- or good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: My name is Daryl Mundis. I'm one of the attorneys representing the Prosecution in this case. I'm going to be asking you some questions. I want to simply make sure that you understand that in the event you don't understand one of my questions, that you feel comfortable enough to tell me so, and I will either rephrase or repeat the question so that you understand. I'm not in any way trying to trick you or get you to say anything that you don't want to say. Let me start by asking just a few questions about the structure of the Territorial Defence that you spoke about. If I understand your testimony correctly, at the top would be the regional Territorial Defence staff, which in 1992 was headquartered in Zenica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Not at the top. The regional Territorial Defence staff wasn't at the top. I just mentioned one organisational level. I said that the district staff was part of the municipal staff, whereas the municipal staff was held accountable by the regional staff which was located in Zenica. There was also a republican staff with its headquarters in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Just so that we're clear, then, the republican Territorial Defence staff was in Sarajevo. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the next level down would be the regional Territorial Defence staff in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Followed by the municipal defence staff in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As far as Travnik Municipality is concerned, each municipality had its own municipal staff, and that included Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And within the municipal defence staff, such as the Travnik municipal defence staff, that was further broken down into districts, district staffs within the municipal defence staffs.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were these district staffs or sector staffs, and there were independent detachments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And I take it from your last answer that the independent detachments were a further subdivision of the district staffs?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: They weren't independent. Well, they were independent, but they had to -- they were held accountable, directly accountable, to the municipal staff, not to the district or sector staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Just for our benefit here, do you recall in 1992 how many districts or how many district staffs there were within the Travnik municipal defence staff?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't say exactly how many of them there were. There was the Travnik district or sector staff. There was the Turbe district staff in the Bila Valley. There were perhaps one or two district staffs. There was the Karaula Independent Detachment. I don't know the exact structure. It's difficult for me to describe the structure exactly as it was. But the district staff of Travnik was active in the area of the town of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And I believe, sir, that you told us that the district staff in Travnik became the 312th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. The Travnik district staff became part of the 312th Brigade. It became part of one of the battalions of the 312th Brigade. And at the time, I think that the brigade had four battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know whether the other district staffs within the Travnik municipal Territorial Defence similarly became either brigades or battalions of brigades within the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as the district staffs are concerned, and as far as these independent detachments are concerned, an order was issued assigning them to various brigades, either to the 312th or to the 306th Brigade. We only had two brigades in the territory of Travnik Municipality. So according to the establishment, they had been assigned there. But since those units were being transformed at the time, not all the men moved into other units. Quite a few of them went to join the police or other units so that the establishment, or rather the district staffs did join up, but not all the men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, sir, that at some point in 1993, all of the components of the Travnik municipal defence staff, the formal organs of that staff, became parts of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: With regard to Travnik Municipality, I'll answer you in certain terms. The district staffs and the independent detachments from the territory of the Municipality of Travnik became part of the 312th and the 306th Brigades, but they didn't enter these brigades as the organisational units of the staff. The organisational structures of the brigades was quite different. So they were reassigned on the basis of that structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know the approximate time period when that happened? Month, or month and year, or time period?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was in November or December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, you also were asked some questions earlier this morning about the war presidency. And you told us that it was difficult for the civilians, since they did not have absolute control over the Territorial Defence after the elections. Is that what you told us this morning?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't understand how it could have been difficult for the civilians. I don't understand your question. Are you referring to the structure of civilian power or are you referring to the civilian population itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, I believe in response to a question, you were asked the composition of the war presidency and whether the commander of the Territorial Defence was part of the war presidency. And in response to that, you made a distinction between the period before the elections and the period after the elections. Let's start at that point. Did the situation change following the elections with respect to the composition of the war presidency?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did. And I've already said in what way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Exactly. Now, do you recall the election that you've referred to, what the time period of that election was? In other words, when did in change in the composition of the war presidency take place?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The change took place after those elections, after the organs of power had been established. Because the functions that were part of the presidency no longer existed. So there were new functions. For example, the president of the club of delegates, deputies, they became part of the composition, whereas the commander of the municipal staff didn't become part of the war presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: My question, sir, is when was that election? The election that you're referring to, what was the date, or the month and the year, of that election to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The elections in Bosnia at the time? Well, that was in 1991 if I'm not mistaken. Perhaps in October. I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It was prior to the war in Bosnia; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was prior to the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You were shown a document earlier, sir, and it was number 656 in the binder of material that you have next to you. And if you would like to turn to it, that's fine. It was the document that was signed by both Ahmed Kulenovic and Filip Filipovic. I believe it was Document 2 in Category 2.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you have that document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At the time this document was produced, sometime in January 1993, would it be fair to say that the Bosnian Muslim armed forces and the HVO were still operating jointly in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, the armed forces were not operating jointly in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, let me start with this question: This document seems to be a document that was signed by a commander of the BH Army and a commander of the HVO. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And this document relates to what area? Does it relate to Travnik? Does it relate to Zenica? Does it relate to some other area? What is the area that this public statement refers to?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: This statement refers to the area of the town of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And there are references in this document, for example, in paragraph 4 where it says "we will jointly prevent..." In paragraph 5 "... we will jointly prevent..." Paragraph 9 refers to "a joint commission." So in January 1993, at least when this document was prepared and signed by both an ABiH commander and an HVO commander, there was some kind of joint cooperation in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: As I said, these were our attempts at cooperating. But they were only attempts. We also decided to form a joint command. And we said that at the head of the command, there should be a Bosniak, and his deputy should be a Croat. We had a meeting and designated the people who were supposed to occupy those positions. Mr. Ribo Haso was supposed to be the commander. His deputy was supposed to be Stojak Ivica from the HVO. However, these were only attempts. And this document is also an attempt. This is just a discussion between officers. And a while ago, I said when examining documents and I mentioned Mr. Bilandzija, we agreed on everything and he attended a meeting at which he gave orders which were contrary to what we had agreed. This is something that I have been able to see on the basis of this documents. And I knew from the field that this was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, would it be fair to characterise this public statement - and I'm referring now to the conclusions section, where there are the nine numbered paragraphs - would it be fair to characterise this is some kind of imposition of martial law?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Martial law? I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, let's --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or rather, the witness said "court-martial." I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'm not referring to a court-martial. I'm referring to a situation where the military authorities are ordering the imposition of a curfew. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: They are issuing an order with respect to the closing times of catering establishments. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Paragraph 5, they indicate that joint steps will be taken to detain, arrest, and disarm if necessary, remove by force all individuals in groups who establish illegal checkpoints. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what it says here. It's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: There's also in paragraph 8 references to the media whereby the military is ordering the media to direct programmes at calming the situation.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, based on these types of steps that were taken by the military officials, that could be interpreted as the imposition of martial law, if you will, if you're familiar with that term.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Such measures, because of the wartime situation, because of the fact that the situation was deteriorating, such measures were taken for this reason. But I would like to point out that if you have a look at this document, you will see that in item 3, which you have quoted but not fully, it says that "a curfew shall be introduced from 2100 hours to 0500 hours. Civilian and military police commanders are responsible for the implementation of the curfew and the appropriate legal measures." So both the civilian and military police are responsible for this. Why? Because the military police can't close down cafes. The civilian organs of power have to do this. The civilian police can close such establishments down but with regard to conscripts, the civilian police cannot deal with them. They can take urgent measures, but they then have to call the military police to take the appropriate measures. So this wartime situation was implemented in the field in this manner. The civilian and military police were active in the field, and each body had its own responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I understand, sir, what you're saying. But the fact of the matter is that the conclusions in this document represent the military authorities ordering the civilian authorities to implement it, does it not, by its very terms of this document?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: This is not an order. This is an enactment which was signed by two commanders on the introduction of a curfew in the presence of the civilian bodies of authorities. With regard to this, at a regular meeting - and now I'm reading from the introduction: "The representative of the BiH Army and the HVO and the meeting was held on the 25th of January 1993 to review the current military, political and security situation in Travnik Municipality in the presence of the prime ministers, Mr. Muhamed Curic and Mr. Zeljko Pervan, and the commanders of the civilian police forces of both sides have arrived at the following conclusions..." This is not an order. These are conclusions that arise from a certain agreement. A curfew was introduced and behaviour was regulated in the territory of the municipality during the daylight and during the curfew.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The fact of the matter is, though, sir that this document was signed by two military commanders, and not by those prime ministers.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The fact is that it was signed by two men who guaranteed the credibility of this document. This document is not an order, and it does not start with the words "hereby I order" or "hereby we order." You have to understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's move on to a different topic. You told us in response to some questions from my learned colleague, Ms. Residovic, you discussed foreigners coming into the Travnik area in the period 1992. Do you remember telling her that or telling us that?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. And I believe that I mentioned all the foreigners whom I saw at the time in the municipality, or rather in the town of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And you told us that you do not remember seeing any armed foreigners in 1992 in Travnik. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Members of the BritBat carried arms. They were armed foreigners. Journalists were not armed. Humanitarians were not armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's talk now about the persons from North Africa or the Middle East. Are you familiar with the term "mujahedin"?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with the term.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you see in the Travnik area in 1992 any persons that might fall within the definition of mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. The mujahedin were -- should have been in uniforms. They should have been armed. I was aware of their presence in the municipality, but I'm referring only to the town area. That's where I moved. I moved towards the line that was my area of responsibility, and in that area there, there were no armed foreigners who would correspond to that description.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. So it's your testimony then, sir, that in 1992 you did not see any mujahedin or armed soldiers or armed forces from Middle Eastern or North African countries in the town of Travnik?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: In the town of Travnik, in the course of 1992, I did not see such armed persons who might be called mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But I believe you've just said that you did see or were aware of such persons in other parts of Travnik Municipality in 1992.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I said I didn't see them, so this is a wrong statement. I did not see them in any other parts of the municipality. But I had information that there were such people in other parts of the municipality. In the urban part of Travnik, I never saw them, and I didn't see them in the part outside the Travnik Municipality proper where I moved about, and that was the area around Ceska Planina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's just -- to clarify this, then, or to take it a step further actually. In 1993 in the town of Travnik, did you see any persons that might be described as mujahedin? I know you've told us about 1992. I'm now asking you about 1993 in the town of Travnik itself. Did you see any persons that might be described as mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: In 1993, I had two encounters with such individuals. Once I saw them passing through town in a car. And on the other occasion, it was in front of a religious building which is very close to my apartment. I don't know when this was, because I did not frankly pay too much attention to these two events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's talk first about the first incident. You saw them passing through town in a car. Do you remember any details such as how many of them were in the car?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I know it was a terrain vehicle. They were in uniforms. They had -- their skin was dark. They did have arms. I can't provide you with any more details. And they passed through town, and this is when I saw them for the first or the second time. I can't even be sure of that. I don't know what was the first encounter. In front of the religious building, there were three of them carrying rifles. And they went up to the entrance into that sacral building, and I did not following their movement any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told us right at the outset of your answer that they were in a terrain vehicle. Can you elaborate on that, or tell us what you meant by a terrain vehicle.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that we are talking about the same thing, a Jeep or a four-wheel drive, an all-terrain vehicle that you might use when you drive around all sorts of terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall what colour the vehicle was or whether the vehicle had any type of markings? Words? Pictures?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: There were no markings, no inscriptions. There were not even registration plates. It was dark. I don't know whether it was dark blue or dark green. Something of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, you told us that you were aware of such individuals. I'm returning now to 1992, sir. You told us that you were aware of mujahedin in Travnik Municipality in places other than the town. You were aware of that in 1992?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: In the area of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's correct. But not in the town of Travnik. Is that right, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: There may have been some of them in the town. I can't deny that. However, the fact is that I myself did not see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's fair enough. I want to ask you, though, when you became aware of them, of the presence of mujahedin in Travnik Municipality outside of the town in 1992, I would like to how you became aware of this. Through what means did you become aware of this?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: In the area of the municipality in the year 1992, there were a lot of armed groups, units, individuals, and we in the command or in our contacts with our friends, we spoke about those different groups, the HOS. Some people were searched. Some people were taken away from their homes and apartments. From Herzegovina, members of the HVO came behaving very arrogantly. And in our stories, we mentioned those armed groups that we now refer to as mujahedin. We didn't call them that at the time. And their appearance and their existence came up in those stories, and that's how we learned that they had appeared in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to put a series of propositions to you, and I would like you to tell us whether you know anything about what I'm talking about or whether you agree or disagree with what I'm going to say to you. Do you understand how this will work? I suggest to you, sir, that beginning in mujahedin, 1992 began entering Bosnia from Croatia for the purpose of engaging the Serbian forces who were attacking the Bosniak population.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Am I supposed to say something, to answer this? Or am I supposed to just listen to your statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I will ask you if based on what I have just put to you you have any comments, any knowledge, whether you had heard anything to this effect, whether you knew anything to this effect. Simply, I want you to tell me based on what I just mentioned, your reaction; whether you knew anything about it, had heard that, knew anything about it, et cetera. And I can repeat the proposition if you would like me to.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No need. I do have the information that certain groups arrived in Bosnia. Whether they came from Croatia, I don't know. But yes, I knew that they came wishing to engage the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And in the early part of the war in Bosnia, that is, late spring, early summer of 1992, the Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat populations were jointly under attack from the Serbs. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So to the extent that the mujahedin who entered Bosnia were primarily going to engage the Serb forces, that would have been in the interests of both the Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat populations, would it not?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Since they wanted to defend Bosnia, obviously it was in the best interests of both populations. This is just my opinion. This is not an official position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, I understand that, sir. You're here to testify as Hamed Mesanovic, not as an official of the Bosnian government or the canton of Travnik. And of course, during the period 1992 -- throughout the war, in fact, the use of the term Chetnik was a common one among the Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat population. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, for the benefit of the listening population and everyone in the courtroom, what does the term "Chetnik" mean?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Chetniks were the military force which existed during the Second World War and which inflicted a lot of pain to the population. They were specialised in destruction of everything and everybody that existed in the former Yugoslavia during the period between 1941 and 1945. They committed war crimes. They killed people. They wore very outstanding clothes, black uniforms, hats, cockades with a skull. And I know all about them from literature and films. Draza Mihajlovic was the Chetnik leader. He was pronounced a war criminal and convicted, I believe. I believe he was sentenced to the death penalty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, in the context of the war in Bosnia in the 1990s, to whom did the term Chetnik apply?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: It was used for the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So based on the responses that you've given us to the last six or seven questions, would it be fair to say that the mujahedin came to Bosnia to fight the Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you're leading me to say that this was the case. I did not have any contacts with the mujahedin. I did not talk to them to ask them why they had come. I didn't ask them whether they would fight and against whom. And at this moment, as I sit here, I don't even think that it was a good thing that they had come in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But again, sir, I suggest to you that the mujahedin came to Bosnia to fight the Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Probably. I can't confirm this. I can just assume that this was the reason. I did not have any contacts with them. I did not find myself in the position to ask them why they had come.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, do you still have Defence Document 656 in front of you? "Public statement," with the conclusions that we spoke about a few moments ago? Do you still have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would like you to turn to paragraph 4 or look at paragraph 4 of that document.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, this is the order signed jointly by the ABiH commander Kulenovic and the HVO commander Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't know whether this is a wrong word used or a misinterpretation. Page 63, 3, it says that this was an order jointly signed. However, the document as has already been explained by the witness is not an order. It is conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, this document is signed by the BH Army Travnik municipal defence council officer Ahmed Kulenovic and the HVO Travnik Brigade commander Colonel Filip Filipovic. And paragraph 4 states "we will jointly prevent entry into Travnik of all armed units, groups, and individuals except for those who come to fight against the Chetniks." And I suggest to you, sir, that the reference in paragraph 4 of Defence Document 656 relates to the mujahedin. And I ask you if you have any comments in light of that suggestion.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you properly, item 4 refers only to the mujahedin, and that's why it was included in the document. Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'm not saying that it exclusively relates to the mujahedin, but what I am saying is that it says "prevent entry of all armed units, groups, or individuals except for those who come to fight against the Chetniks." And I'm suggesting to you that the phrase "those who come to fight against the Chetniks" refers to the mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: If it referred to the mujahedin, then it would be worded as follows: "except for the mujahedin who arrive here in order to fight against the Chetnik."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Unless, of course, someone did not want to put the word "mujahedin" down in a written document.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I think, since the document was signed by the commanders of the two armies, that in a way that they dictated the wording, that they would have used the word "mujahedin." This applies to all the units that roamed around the town for different reasons, rather than to fight against the Chetniks. They had other reasons to move about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, I suggest to you, sir, and this will be my last question before the technical break - I do have some additional questions after the break - but what I suggest to you, sir, is that this order -- or not order, this documents relates to in paragraph 4 reflects the fact that at the time this document was written, the ABiH and the HVO in their joint fight against the Chetniks were still willing to allow the mujahedin entry into Travnik. If you disagree with that, you can simply say you disagree with it.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot just use one word, but you are wrong, sir. The BiH Army and the HVO were not fighting against the Chetniks jointly. They were never joined. We did have joint commands on paper, but this never took off on the grounds We did not have joint units. And if you think that this applies to the mujahedin, let me elaborate and extend that to, for example, the HOS who also arrived in the town and disrupted law and order. This also applies to the HVO from Herzegovina who did not come for any other reason but to plunder and ill-treat people. They stopped people. They stormed various institutions. They asked whether there were any Serbs there. Their main task was to ill treat and harass people. This also applies to some other groups who occupied abandoned flats, plundered property in those flats. All of these were armed groups who entered the town of Travnik, and their purpose was anything but the fight against the Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I note the time, Mr. President. As I indicated, I do have some remaining questions. And just for the benefit of the Chamber and the Defence, we would again respectfully request that we show this witness the video P762 following the break. This was the same video shown to the first witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will resume at 5 to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, you may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to show you now a videoclip which, with the assistance of the usher, you'll be able to watch on the screen in front of you. Before I show you this, let me just ask you -- or let me explain to you the procedure that we're going to use. We will not have any audio played from the videotape so that the tape you see, there won't be any sound. I would like you to look at the videotape. And during the course of the videotape, if you recognise where the videotape was taken, if you could just tell us. And you don't need to pause. You can simply say where it is as the videotape is playing. If you recognise any person on the videotape, I would ask you immediately to stay "stop," and we will stop the videotape. That avoids having to rewind and find the place on the videotape. So if you see anyone that you recognise, please immediately say "stop," and we'll stop and then I'll ask you who the person or persons that you recognise on the videotape might be. It's possible, of course, that you won't recognise anyone or recognise anything about the videotape, in which case we will all be here in about six minutes of silence. If you can tell us where or if you recognise anyone on the tape, please tell us that as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I see my learned colleague is on her feet, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, first of all, I would like to say that the Prosecution hasn't informed us of their intention to use this video. And although Defence counsel has complied with all its duties in accordance with the Rules and we have provided the Prosecution with all the evidence we will be using, we have -- following your instructions, we provided the Prosecution with all the evidence we were going to use. This is why I want to draw your attention to the use of this video. But in the interests of justice, the main reason for addressing the Trial Chamber is that we don't see the grounds on which Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond the Prosecution wants to use this video. We don't see the reason for doing this. In the course of my examination, no reason arose for which this video might be shown. Similarly, the Prosecution has not informed us of the legal basis on which they want to show the video. So we would be grateful if the Prosecution could provide us with a valid basis for showing this video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the Prosecution like to respond to the comments just made by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. And I would respectfully request to do so in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Usher, could you escort the witness out of the courtroom for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Let me first address the general issue or the first issue that my learned colleague raised. With respect to cross-examination, our position is one which I believe is similar to the position that the Defence had taken in cross-examining witnesses; that is, the party who is calling the witness in our respectful submission is required to give notice as to which documents or exhibits are going to be shown to the witness. But at no point, to my recollection, during the Prosecution case did the Defence ever notify the Prosecution or the Trial Chamber in advance as to what documents they might be using during their cross-examinations, first of all. Second of all, of course, this is a videotape which is in evidence, and therefore our view, of course, is that anything that's already in evidence is subject to use during cross-examination with any witness. And the third point that I would bring up, although, again, I'm hesitant to do so, is that if the Trial Chamber were to take a careful look at the Rule 65 ter summary provided of this witness, there wasn't a great deal of information that led us to believe that this witness would be talking about, among other things, the Muslim forces which he did, in fact, on his direct examination talk about. Coupled with the fact, of course, that we don't have any witness statements of the witnesses, the Prosecution is only able once the witness completes his or her testimony to make rather snap decisions in some cases about what documents, exhibits, videos, maps, et cetera, might be shown to the witness. All we really have to go on are the Rule 65 ter summaries, which are relatively brief. Consequently, if we were to be ordered to give such advance notice, we would be placed in an extremely difficult position. And with respect to many of the witnesses, we would probably have to take some kind of an adjournment in order to prepare those lists and/or to notify the Defence. With respect to this witness and this videotape, the witness has testified about the Muslim forces or the MS during the direct examination. As we explained with the first witness, the Prosecution's theory is that this videotape shows not necessarily the formation of that unit, but part of that unit in the very early period in which it was formed. The first witness to testify about this videotape last week identified it as being in front of the Medresa in Travnik, which is precisely the same location mentioned by this witness earlier this morning. And for purposes of the future Defence witnesses, we would propose showing this same video or other videos to any of the witnesses who can shed light on material contained in the videos. So in effect, I would propose that this is a blanket request of the Prosecution to show the videotapes to any and all Defence witnesses who might be able to shed some light on persons or places, or even time periods that are shown in the videotapes. I thank the Trial Chamber for its consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. With regard to the issue you have raised -- Mr. Bourgon, is there anything you would like to say? I saw you standing up. With regard to this matter, Defence counsel tells us that they weren't informed of the Prosecution's intention to show the witness this video. The Prosecution responded by saying that when they called their own witnesses, you presented documents at the last minute without having informed the Prosecution of your intention to do so. So the same rules should be applied to the Prosecution. And this is part of what we call a fair trial. In the course of its cross-examination, the Prosecution proceeded in this manner, and why shouldn't the Prosecution proceed in the same manner when cross-examining a witness. This video is also in evidence. It has been exhibit number. It has already been shown to a witness who was able to recognise the events depicted in the video. And thirdly, the witness who appeared before this one mentioned the Medresa, and this witness appearing here today also mentioned the Medresa, and he mentioned a unit that was billeted there. And as a result, the Prosecution will be asking the witness whether the place that he mentioned was, in fact, the place where these people were. But in any event, it was my intention to show this video to the witness because this witness told us, and you shouldn't forget this, that he almost never saw mujahedin. He heard about them. He heard that some of them were at the outskirts of the town. He met some on two occasions. But the outcome is that the mujahedin more or less were men who were quite unfamiliar to this witness. We can ask ourselves whether the witness actually saw them or didn't see them, and this is why it might be interesting to show the witness this video. This would enable us to determine the truth. It would be in the interests of justice to proceed in this manner. We have lost ten minutes now, but let's call the witness back into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you understand exactly the procedure that we'll be using in watching the videotape?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask now that Prosecution Exhibit 762 be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see anything. The quality of the image is very poor. But I think I can recognise the furniture salon in Travnik which was also known as the Medresa. Yes, in fact, it is the Medresa. I think that this person is the Travnik Mufti, although I've never seen him dressed in this manner. Could you continue showing the video.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is the Travnik Mufti. Efendi Nusret Avdibegovic. I can see him well now. Could you pause there, please. This person here, I'm not quite certain, but I think this is someone called Mektauf from Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, if I could ask you for the benefit of the transcript to describe the person that you believe is Mr. Mektauf, including perhaps what he's wearing, where he is in the video in the frame that you see before you, et cetera. And tell us which person you're referring to, please.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: In this image, it's the person in the middle of the frame. He's wearing a T-shirt. It's a camouflage T-shirt or an imitation of such a T-shirt. He's got short hair, and he has a beard. Part of it is a little longer, and part of it is a little shorter. Is that sufficient?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. While we're on this frame, if you could, there are other individuals that are visible who appear to be wearing military uniforms. And I would ask you if you recognise any of the insignia on any of the uniforms that you see on this still frame that's before you right now. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I can see that they have insignia on them, but I can't recognise them. But the video is a very poor quality. It's very difficult to discern the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd ask that the video be shown to its conclusion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here I can see some individuals in white robes. As I said, when the humanitarian -- when representatives of humanitarian organisations first started arriving, they were dressed in a similar manner. And this is why I said that they were from those countries, from these Arab countries or African countries. It doesn't mean that these are such persons. It's not very clear, but I'm talking about the clothes that they're wearing. They wore distinctive clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, you've identified two individuals on this tape and the location of the tape. I'm wondering if you have any other information or you can tell us anything else about what was shown in the videotape.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: It's obvious that the video was shot in Travnik, and I can see on the basis of the date that it was in August 1992 that it was shot. It was shot in Travnik in front of the furniture salon, also known as the Medresa. And when I compare these dates, this was probably the video of the establishment of this Muslim unit in the town of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you say "this Muslim unit in the town of Travnik," are you referring to the Muslimanske Snage, MS?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, some people call them the Muslim forces. Some people call them the Muslim unit. But that's more or less what it was. This unit was composed of young men from the area of Travnik Municipality. I can't say whether they were just from that territory or whether they were from other municipalities, too, or whether there were any refugees in that unit. I saw such people in the town, and on the whole this is the unit I am referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned the person you identified as Mr. Avdibegovic. Do you know what Mr. Avdibegovic did during the war?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Avdibegovic was a member of the clergy. I don't know exactly what he did at the beginning. But I think he was an imam in the Sarina mosque in Travnik. And in 1993, he became, or rather he was elected as the Travnik Mufti. Elections were held.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And for the benefit of everyone in the courtroom, can you just briefly explain, if you know, what a Mufti is.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you must understand me. I don't understand the religious hierarchy very well because I'm not someone who is religious. But I know that there is someone who is responsible for a certain mosque, and he performs certain rites, whereas a Mufti is a high-ranking member of the clergy and he covers an area which is called a Muftiluk. I don't know if that would be the right term. And he is responsible for the religious work in that area. And the headquarters of the Travnik Mufti are in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So it's fair to say, then, that a Mufti is a religious leader of some standing and education. Would that be a fair characterisation?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't say leader. I said a religious cleric, a member of the clergy of a certain level. And I can't really provide you with much information about this, but you could probably ask people who are more familiar with these matters. They could tell you what sort of a level this is and who he is above and who is under him. But I'm not really competent to comment on these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Avdibegovic, as a Mufti, someone learned in the Koran, would speak Arabic, would he not?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He would speak Arabic, and I think he even finished religious school somewhere abroad, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's turn now to the other person you identified, Mr. Mektauf. What can you tell us about him?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mektauf, well, I know that he's a citizen of Travnik Municipality. He went to university in Sarajevo. He got married in Travnik. He was involved in trade. Before he had a video club, and then he started trading in technical goods. He built some buildings in Travnik, some residential buildings and office premises. I know he got divorced, and he had a big company in Travnik which was involved in trade. And through the media, I know that certain police measures were taken against him, and I don't know whether criminal proceedings were instituted against him. But an investigation was launched because he was accused of being involved in drug trafficking in the postwar period. Nothing was proven, though; nothing was found. And then proceedings were instituted again because he failed to pay duty. And this came to nothing as far as I know, as far as a prosecution is concerned. The last thing I heard was that he was arrested in Sarajevo. He was charged with having committed white-collar crime and with having taken away by force Croats and one Serb from Travnik in the course of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned Mr. Mektauf having a video club. Do you know or recall the name of that video club and where it was located?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: His video club was located in the upper part of the town, in the vicinity of the former cinema. This cinema has closed down now. But I can't remember the name of the video club. Perhaps if someone reminded me, I would be able to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me move on. I have just a few remaining questions, sir. You mentioned earlier the two instances where you saw the mujahedin. And on one of those instances, you mentioned that they were in a vehicle. And the English transcript also indicates that you said that they were wearing uniforms. Can you verify that they were, in fact, wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were in uniform. They weren't wearing the white clothes I have mentioned, and they weren't wearing civilian clothes either. They were in uniform. I don't know whether they had complete uniforms on them. I saw some sort of a jacket. I don't know whether they had the trousers on them, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And sir, when you say "uniform," I assume that that would be a military uniform that they were wearing, some kind of military uniform.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to clothing, to some kind of camouflage clothing. As to whether it was the military uniform of some regular army force, I couldn't say. But they were wearing camouflage clothes. And I'm only talking about what I saw in the jeep when they were passing by. As to whether they were all wearing camouflage clothes, I don't know. But on the basis of what I could see at the time, those people were wearing such clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And sir, you also told us earlier that in 1993, the 306th Brigade and the 312th Brigades were in the town of Travnik. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I suggest to you, sir, that in addition to those two brigade, a battalion of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade was also in Travnik. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I want to avoid confusion. This is nothing that I have not claimed already. I just replied to the questions, and I said that the 306th and the 312th Brigades had been established in the territory of Travnik Municipality and that they incorporated members from the units that I mentioned. I did not mention the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade, which was in Travnik. That is a different thing. The 7th Battalion [as interpreted] composed of the members who were Bosniaks who were on the strength of this battalion -- actually, some Bosniaks, because this unit, this Muslim unit that was established had a very strange history. They were never incorporated either in the 306th or the 312th Brigades. They were not incorporated on the strength of the anti-sabotage units of the municipal staff. They were incorporated in the 7th Muslim Brigade, but not all of them. The headquarters of that brigade was in Zenica, so some of them did join the 306th. The others did join the 312th. Some joined the police. Some became sort of independent and they didn't go anywhere. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond You may continue asking me questions, though. Maybe I can elaborate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Page 76, line 11 -- lines 10 and 11 makes reference to the 7th Battalion. Was that, in fact, the 7th Brigade, the 1st Battalion of the 7th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I said the 1st Batallion of the 7th Brigade. And it was not my mistake. I suppose it was misinterpreted, my words were misinterpreted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, do you know in what time period in 1993 the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade was in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade, I don't know whether -- the complete one. But in any case, some of its members were there in 1993, at the beginning of June when the conflict broke out with the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know who in 1993, or at least in the beginning of June 1993, when that battalion was in Travnik, do you know who the commander of that battalion was?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that their commander was a man from Krajina who later on became a brigadier. I can't remember his name. I know him well, however. And I believe that he was the commander of the 1st Battalion. Maybe he was commander before the battalion was established. I really don't know. In any case, I know that he was a man from Krajina, but I don't know whether it was before the battalion was established or after the battalion was established. I can't be sure. It may come to me still.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Fair enough, sir. And I certainly don't want you to speculate if you don't recall. Let me just ask you a final question on this subject: You mentioned that the formation of this battalion had as -- I think the words are now gone, but you said a strange history. I'm wondering if you can elaborate or explain a little bit more about your knowledge as to the establishment of the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, this battalion that was in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Why a strange history? I don't know that many details about the establishment of this battalion or who established it. I had my zone of responsibility on the Sesici mountain, and I was constantly fighting against the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressor. I was responsible for the logistical support. We had various cease-fires, exchanges of the dead and wounded because of the refugees who were passing through the Vlasic plateau. I heard that this unit was being established, and it was inconceivable to me that we could not bring our unit to the strength. We did not have enough equipment for ourselves, and all of a sudden a new unit was being established. So my mind, it was just a way to move some people away from the fighting. These people were then assigned to various defence lines. Again, I would speculate if I said it was Karaula. I can't be sure of that. Then they were linked up with the Zenica unit, which is not logical. At the same time, we had two brigades in Travnik that we could not bring to strength. So all this was rather strange. In any case, there were other people who also didn't understand that they were members of that unit, but they said "what am I supposed to do in Zenica?" Then they left this unit and they joined either the 306th or 311th Brigades. Nobody came to me because I had nothing to do with religion, as I've already said. And I know that some of these men also became sort of independent agents. They didn't want to join anybody. They just sort of decided to separate from any organised unit and became independent, and that's how they acted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, earlier on today, page 20, line 9, you made reference to the Croatian Army. Do you remember using that term?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I said that I don't have that particular page in front of me. I know that I mentioned at the very beginning this was not the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council at the very beginning, but it was rather the Croatian Army. I was not referring to the Croatian state. I was referring to the unit that consisted of Croats. That's why I said that it was the Croatian Army. It was only later on that they gave themselves a proper name, the Croatian Defence Council. They designed their own logo and insignia. They advertised themselves on TV. Actually, both armies advertised themselves on TV trying to prompt people to join them. And that's why I said at the beginning they were the Croatian Army, not the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you make a distinction, sir, between the Croatian Defence Council as being a force of Bosnian Croats and the Croatian Army as being persons from the Republic of Croatia? Are you making that distinction in this terminology?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The Croatian Army that is active in Croatia, and some of its units later on entered Bosnia. That is one body of the military. On the other hand, we have the Croatian Defence Council which was the official army of the so-called Croatian Community of Herceg Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Just so that we're all clear here, sir, the HVO refers to the Croatian Defence Council which was composed of Bosnian Croats; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Bosnian Croats. There were also volunteers from abroad, but again, we're talking about Bosnian Croats who used to live in Bosnia and then went on to work abroad, and then they joined the HVO. The HVO were units which were not typical only of Travnik, but of other places, Busovaca, Zenica. Now, what type of system they had, whether they recruited their men just from Travnik if they were the HVO of Travnik, or whether they recruited them from other parts of Bosnia, I wouldn't know. But this is what I refer to, Bosnian Croats, when I say the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you say the Croatian Army, which is also known as the HV, that's the Army of the Republic of Croatia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honour, I believe that the witness has already replied, and he said that at the beginning before the HVO was established, Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina used to call their groups the Croatian Army. But again, we are talking of one and the same thing. And the witness said he made a clear distinction between the Croatian Army from the Croatian state and those that initially called themselves the Croatian Army and later on began the HVO. I don't understand why my learned friend insists on putting the witness one and the same question again and again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm simply doing it because the transcript -- the English transcript is not as clear as it might be to my learned colleague who is listening in the native language. If the Defence is of the view that the Croatian Army was present in Bosnia in 1993, that's fine. But I'm simply trying to clarify the record as it exists at least with respect to the English transcript that is appearing on the screen in front of me and which is not as clear as my learned colleague, as it seems to be to her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence, what would you like to say to this?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't see here that a question was put as to the presence of the Croatian Army in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Defence has never dealt with that issue. The witness himself spoke about some groups that existed before the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and he said that some local Croats called themselves the Croatian Army, and that immediately after that, they changed their name and started calling themselves the HVO. And the witness has already said that twice. This is on page 79, line 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please clarify very quickly, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, when you've made reference to the Croatian Army, are you referring to the HV? That is, the Army of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know what contexts are we dealing with. Let me try and explain to avoid any confusion. At the beginning Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond of the war, the HVO did not exist. Croats gathered in groups. They were armed, and they called themselves the Croatian Army. After that, the HVO was officially established. And these Croats started wearing the insignia of the Croatian Defence Council that they belonged to. Those people were Bosniaks, Croats who resided in the territory of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And sir, did you just say a few moments ago that later on, the Croatian Army entered Bosnia? Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And this is a fact. Operations around Kljuc, operations around Kupres, operations around Bosanska Krajina, Mrkonjic Grad, Jajce. It was the Croatian Army that was involved in all that. I'm sure that you are aware of those things. The Croatian Army did all that, and the Croatian Defence Council only followed the Croatian Army to occupy the territory, and they never took part in the actual combat operations. They just followed the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, sir, for purposes of clarification, what are you talking about when you say "the Croatian Army"?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The Croatian Army is the armed force of the state of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time. The only remaining thing I would ask to do is we do have a still of the -- of one part of the video that the witness has already identified. It's a still photograph of Mr. Avdibegovic along with one other individual. I would ask that the witness be shown that and that he identify by marking on the still photograph the person he identified on the videotape. We can either do that now or first thing in the morning. I have no further questions once the witness has made that identification and signed and dated the photograph and of course we would tender that into evidence. But we have nothing further to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Theoretically, we should have concluded today's session a few minutes ago. Did the Defence want to re-examine the witness? If that is the case, we will have to ask the witness to come back tomorrow morning. At this moment, the Judges did not want to put any questions to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if we can stay for 10 minutes more, the Defence might have one or two questions in re-examination after the Prosecution's cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the counsel repeat what he said because the mic was not on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpreters did not hear you, sir. Can you please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we do not have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we can deal with everything in the next few minutes. Mr. Mundis, go on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If that's the case, Mr. President, I would ask again that this still photograph from the video --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please show it to the Defence counsel. And show it to the accused as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And while they're doing that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, if you could, once the photograph is placed before you, if you could mark the person by writing his name, the person that you've identified as Mr. Avdibegovic.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Actually, I would ask, sir, if you would just take a marker and write the name of that individual somewhere on the photograph. Perhaps...

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And then, sir, if you could perhaps draw a line to the person that you've identified so it's clear to everyone which person you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, with the remark that I'm not sure whether the second letter is a V or a B. I don't know whether his family name is Avdibegovic or Avdibegovic. In any case, this is the person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And draw please, all the way to him -- it's the person holding the megaphone?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the person holding the megaphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Finally, sir, if you could with a small marker in the lower right-hand corner, sign your name and place today's date, which is the 27th of October 2004.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Mr. President, we would tender that into evidence at the appropriate time. The Prosecution has no further questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other one whom he recognised, you don't have a still of that? You don't want to do anything with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. We don't have a still of that exact person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you want to tender this photo into evidence. You want a number? Mr. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The photo is admitted as P932.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The re-examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have just two questions, as I've said. I would like the witness to be shown Document DH29. In order to speed up the procedure, I have the document with me. It is a decree from the Official Gazette of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is the decree law on defence. Can the witness please be shown this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mesanovic, can you please look at page 8, Article 40. Page 8, Article 40. To my learned friend's question, you responded and talked about the composition of the war presidency.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please read this article.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: "The presidency of the municipality is composed of the president of the municipality, president of the executive council, the chief of the ministry, the chief of the public security station, the commander of the territorial staff, and presidents of the groups of deputies in the municipal assembly."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is this a regulation that regulated the composition of the war presidency of which you spoke of earlier on?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is the regulation which regulates its composition.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This document has already been admitted into evidence. My second question is to do with the explanations you gave my learned friend about the presence of the Croatian Army units when certain territories were being liberated. Can you please tell me, what year was that when these territories were liberated and whether the Croatian Army then acted as the Army of the state which was cooperating with the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. An agreement had been reached at the state level. And according to that agreement, the Croatian Army as the ally of Bosnia-Herzegovina participated in the activities on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina in order to push the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressor away.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What year was that?

utterances.speaker: HAMED MESANOVIC
utterances.text: It was in 1994 or 1995. I'm not sure. In any case, this was during those particular combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if nobody else has any questions to put to the witness, I would like to thank the witness. Thank you very much for having come to testify. We have exceeded the Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond time. We wish you a good journey back home, and we wish you our best for -- in your professional career. I'm going to ask the usher to accompany you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the Defence wants to tell us something about the schedule of witnesses to come. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as I have already emphasised on several occasions, there may be some problems with travel documents and visas for some of our witnesses. The first reason for which is the fact that the majority of our witnesses do not have passports; and secondly, we grouped our witness around the topics, and we informed our witnesses accordingly. That's how they applied for passports. Thirdly, we had to reschedule our initial schedule because of the decision that General Merdan would be called at a different time, and he was supposed to testify over the period of at least ten days. We have provided the schedule for up to the 12th of November. However, earlier on, the Victims and Witnesses Unit informed us that the Embassy of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in Sarajevo cannot issue visas for Mr. Dervis Suljic and Hamed Suljic until next Thursday, so they will not be able to appear before next Thursday. Since Zijad Sehic and Sulejman Ribo have already got visas, we are going to call these witnesses in the following order: First, Zijad Sehic, and then Sulejman Ribo. However, since the witnesses Dervis and Hamed Suljic will not be able to arrive in order to appear on Wednesday, there is a high probability that we will not be able to call any other witnesses for Wednesday. Instead of that, Witnesses Enes Ribic and the other witness will appear on Thursday and Friday. I am not familiar with the reasons, however, the Victims and Witnesses Unit has informed us that they asked the Embassy to try and issue the visas for our witnesses before Monday morning so as to enable them to travel, however, that all of their efforts were to no avail. For these reasons, I regret to say that despite all of our efforts, on Wednesday we will not be able to have a witness. And we already know that Suad Menzil cannot obtain a passport, and that's why we have added a new witness to the list. He already has a passport. Is his name is Sead Jusic. Save for these few witnesses, the remainder of the list remains the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood you well, we have the expert. On Tuesday, Mr. Ribo. On Wednesday for the time being, there is nobody. And you are hoping that on Thursday, you will be able to bring two witnesses as per the schedule. And on Friday, Mr. Jusic probably.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel. Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On Friday, we will have Mr. -- I can't say exactly. Maybe Jusic Haris and Sejad, or maybe Enes Ribic. This will all depend on the organisation put together by the Victims and Witness Unit. In any case, we will have a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question to you: Tomorrow, Thursday, we have a witness who has been scheduled, and the -- there is a witness. However, we have learned that maybe tomorrow we'll have two witnesses, in theory. Do you think that you will have enough time tomorrow to hear two witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I can say that I will need not more than an hour and a half for the first witness. However, so far, the cross-examination has taken as much time, if not more. I don't know how long might it take tomorrow. The practice so far tells me that the second witness will be able to start his testimony, but I'm also sure that it will not be able to finish tomorrow. I don't know what the possibilities are for Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar, do we have a courtroom available on Friday in the morning or in the afternoon? It will be best if we had a courtroom available in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll discuss the matter tomorrow. It seems that the courtrooms will be occupied. So if we have to continue on Friday, it will be necessary to do so in the afternoon, unless one of the hearings is cancelled; this happens occasionally. If that is the case, we'll be able to have a hearing on Friday morning. The other solution is to hear both witnesses -- to finish with both witnesses tomorrow, if you proceed efficiently. You may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I really cannot undertake to finish examining both witnesses by the end of tomorrow's hearing. But perhaps there would be a courtroom available tomorrow afternoon, in which case we could continue working in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As your suggestion is quite appropriate, we could continue working tomorrow afternoon. And the Registrar tells us that this is possible. So we will take steps to make sure that we can continue in the afternoon. If there are no other issues to raise, I will see everyone at the hearing that will start tomorrow at 9.00. And I apologise to the interpreters for having taken 20 additional minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
